newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil vows to push ahead but mining sale in limbo.
newsitem.headline: Brazil vows to push ahead but mining sale in limbo.

text.p: Brazil pledged to push ahead with the sale of the state mining company CVRD, but the biggest sale of state-owned assets in Latin American history remained on hold as a judge delayed ruling on legal challenges.

Superior Court Justice Democrito Ramos Reinaldo asked for 10 more days to consider his verdict, a court spokesman said, thereby leaving in place lower court rulings temporarily blocking the sale of Companhia Vale do Rio Doce, or CVRD.
The government has been awaiting a ruling from the Superior Court on an appeal asking that various lower court rulings blocking the sale should be referred to a single tribunal.
"This is not a defeat. We always knew we would have to fight this one in the courts," Planning Minister Antonio Kandir said in a televised interview before the judge delayed his ruling.
"What is important is that the auction should take place, and the sooner the better."
In a separate TV interview, Kandir said he hoped the auction could still be held this week or at the latest next week.

Forty-five percent of CVRD's voting stock was to be auctioned on the Rio de Janeiro stock exchange on Tuesday but the government failed to have all 21 court injunctions suspending the auction revoked.

The sale of CVRD, the world's largest iron ore producer and exporter, would be the biggest sale of state assets in Latin America, and was expected to net the government at least $5 billion if completed.

The company has a reputation for efficiency, which is rare for a state-owned enterprise. It also owns the world's largest iron ore deposit, which holds 18 billion metric tons, located in the Carajas mining region in the Amazon state of Para.
The court spokesman said the judge had given the government 10 days to provide the information needed for the ruling but noted that could be shortened.

"The (government) could speed up the delivery of the information. The judge has given them 10 days for that," he said. Asked if this meant the privatisation was off for the time being, the spokesman said, "Yes."

The judge had been considering a government petition that argued a series of injunctions against the sell-off should be handled by a single court because of a "conflict of interpretation" in lower courts.
Two groups are ready to bid in the sale: one is led by Brazilian steelmaker CSN, the other by local metal, cement and pulp producer Votorantim and South Africa's Anglo-American Corp.
"This (legal problems) is no surprise. It's just part of the democratic process," Votorantim Chief Executive Antonio Ermirio de Moraes said in a television interview.
Local newspapers reported Wednesday that Brazilian pulp and paper group Cia. Suzano had pulled out of the CSN-led consortium but this could not be immediately confirmed.

Opponents of the sale, ranging from former Presidents Jose Sarney and Itamar Franco to Brazil's Catholic bishops, have accused the government of selling the country's mineral wealth to foreigners for a pittance.

The legal battle against the sale was mirrored outside the Rio de Janeiro stock exchange on Tuesday when about 2,000 leftist protesters clashed with riot police. Authorities said about 29 people were injured.
There were no protesters in sight Wednesday and the area remained calm.
